Partial Preterism
PAR-shul PREE-ter-iz-um
n. phrase (eschatological position; the view that the majority of New Testament prophecy — including the Olivet Discourse and most of Revelation — was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, while the Second Coming and Final Resurrection remain future)
Partial from Latin partialis, from pars (part); indicating that only part of the prophetic material is held to have been fulfilled, as distinct from full or hyper-preterism. Preterism from Latin praeteritus (past), from praeterire (to go past, pass by); the view that the events prophesied have already passed. The “partial” qualifier distinguishes this position from full preterism (which holds even the Resurrection and Second Coming to be past events), which Reformed confessional theology unanimously rejects as outside the bounds of orthodoxy.

Biblical Definition

Partial preterism is the eschatological interpretation that holds that the bulk of New Testament prophecy — particularly the Olivet Discourse of Matthew 24, Mark 13, and Luke 21, and the greater part of the book of Revelation — was fulfilled in and around the Roman siege and destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. Matthew 24:34 is the interpretive pivot: “Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.” Partial preterists read “this generation” as referring to the first-century Jewish generation, making the fulfillment of most of Matthew 24:4–34 events of the years AD 66–70. Revelation 1:1 supports this: “the things that must shortly take place” — and Revelation 1:3 adds: “for the time is near.” Partial preterism reads these temporal markers as genuine first-century time references, not timeless or symbolic. Distinguished from full (or hyper-) preterism, partial preterism affirms that the physical, bodily Second Coming of Christ, the bodily resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment remain as future literal events — thus remaining within the bounds of Nicene orthodoxy. Major partial preterist voices in the Reformed tradition include R.C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus), Kenneth Gentry, and Gary DeMar. The Westminster Confession and 1689 LBCF are eschatologically flexible on this question; partial preterism is a legitimate position within the confessional Reformed tradition.

Webster 1828 Definition

The eschatological view that most New Testament prophecy — especially the Olivet Discourse and most of Revelation — was fulfilled in the AD 70 destruction of Jerusalem, while the Second Coming, Resurrection, and Final Judgment remain as future, literal events; a legitimate position within confessional Reformed eschatology.

PARTIAL PRETERISM, n. phrase. The interpretation of New Testament prophecy that places the fulfillment of most prophetic material in the first century AD — specifically, in the events surrounding the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple in AD 70 — while retaining the bodily Second Coming, bodily Resurrection of the dead, and Final Judgment as future literal events. The “partial” qualifier is essential: it distinguishes this position from full preterism, which denies any future eschatological events, and which Reformed confessional theology uniformly rejects.

Matthew 24:34 (“this generation will not pass away until all these things take place”) and Revelation 1:1, 3 (“things which must shortly take place”; “the time is near”) are the textual anchors. Partial preterists read these temporal markers as genuine first-century time references: Jesus was predicting the fall of Jerusalem within the lifetime of His hearers, and John was writing to seven first-century churches about events imminently approaching them. The alternative — that “shortly” and “near” mean 2,000+ years hence — requires hermeneutical gymnastics that partial preterism argues are unnecessary.

The major literary case for partial preterism in the modern Reformed world is R.C. Sproul's The Last Days According to Jesus (1998), which argues from the time-text evidence that the “last days” language of the New Testament refers to the last days of the Old Covenant economy — the period from Christ's ascension to the Temple's destruction. Kenneth Gentry's Before Jerusalem Fell (1989) argues for an early date of Revelation (pre-AD 70) to support the same conclusion.

Partial preterism is compatible with amillennialism (which it most naturally pairs with), with postmillennialism (with some adjustment), and with certain historic premillennial readings. It is not compatible with classical dispensationalism, which requires the majority of Revelation's events to be future. The 1689 LBCF and Westminster Confession do not specify among these options, making partial preterism a legitimate intra-confessional position.

Full or hyper-preterism (which holds the Second Coming and Resurrection to have already occurred spiritually in AD 70) is outside the bounds of orthodox Christianity; it denies the Apostles' Creed's “He shall come again to judge the living and the dead.” No confessional Reformed body accepts full preterism as within the pale.

Key Scripture

Matthew 24:34 — "Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place."

Luke 21:32 — "Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all things take place."

Revelation 1:1 — "The Revelation of Jesus Christ — which God gave Him to show to His bondservants the things that must shortly take place."

Revelation 1:3 — "Blessed is the one who reads, and those who hear the words of this prophecy and keep what is written in it — for the time is near."

Modern Corruption

Full or hyper-preterism extends partial preterism's first-century fulfillment to include the Second Coming and Resurrection, placing these events in AD 70 and thus departing from every historic creed and confession; meanwhile, popularized dispensationalism misreads “this generation” as a reference to a future generation that sees the signs, contorting the natural meaning of the text.

expand to see more

Full preterism — associated with Max King, Don Preston, and the Covenant Eschatology movement — extends the preterist logic to its terminus: if most prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, then the Second Coming and Resurrection must have occurred spiritually in AD 70 as well. This conclusion is incompatible with every historic Christian creed. The Apostles' Creed affirms: “He will come again to judge the living and the dead.” The Nicene Creed: “He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and His kingdom will have no end.” The 1689 LBCF (32–33) affirms a bodily resurrection and a future final judgment. Full preterism is not a legitimate option within confessional Christianity, regardless of its hermeneutical energy. No Reformed denomination accepts it.

Dispensational popular eschatology takes the opposite error: reading “this generation” in Matthew 24:34 as a reference to a future generation that witnesses the signs of the Great Tribulation (signs that dispensationalism places entirely in a seven-year period preceding Christ's return). This requires the word “generation” (genea) to mean something it never means elsewhere in Matthew (where it consistently refers to the contemporaries of Jesus — e.g., Matt 11:16; 12:39, 41, 42, 45; 23:36). The dispensational reading protects a future-fulfillment scheme at the cost of natural exegesis; partial preterism reads the text straightforwardly and allows the time texts to mean what they say.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Partial preterism traces to the early church (Eusebius), was given its modern Reformed articulation by Moses Stuart, and has been recovered by R.C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry, and Gary DeMar as a serious exegetical alternative within the confessional Reformed tradition.

expand to see more

Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History (c. AD 313) — the earliest sustained reading of Matthew 24 as fulfilled in the AD 70 siege; Eusebius reads the Olivet Discourse as a detailed prophecy of the events Josephus records in The Jewish War.

Moses Stuart, Commentary on the Apocalypse (1845) — the nineteenth-century American scholarly recovery of preterist exegesis; Stuart's work laid the exegetical groundwork for later Reformed preterist readings.

R.C. Sproul, The Last Days According to Jesus (1998) — the most accessible modern Reformed case; Sproul argues that the time-text evidence is so strong that any honest reading of Matthew 24 must take the first-century fulfillment seriously.

Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell (1989) — the technical argument for a pre-AD 70 date of Revelation; if Revelation was written under Nero, its “imminent” language refers to events that were, from the author's perspective, genuinely near.

1689 LBCF, Chapters 32–33 (Of the State of Man after Death / Of the Last Judgment) — the confessional limits: bodily resurrection of all the dead, a final judgment of all persons, and the eternal states of heaven and hell; these remain future and literal on every orthodox eschatological reading.

Usage

"Partial preterism does not deny the Second Coming or Final Judgment; it relocates most of Matthew 24 to the past, which actually clarifies the future hope — the return of Christ is no longer mixed up with first-century siege language but stands distinct as a future, glorious, unconditioned event."

"The strongest argument for partial preterism is the simplest: Jesus said “this generation” would see all these things, and “this generation” in every other use in Matthew means the contemporaries of Jesus — the burden of proof falls on those who give it any other meaning."

"Pastors should distinguish partial preterism from full preterism clearly: the former is within the confessional Reformed tradition and deserves a fair hearing; the latter denies the bodily return of Christ and the future bodily resurrection and falls outside the bounds of historic Christian orthodoxy."
